I'm mapping out the cell coordinates for each numbered shape - shape 5 with 3 cells, shape 7 with 4 cells, shapes 2 and 3 each with 5 cells, and shape 8 with 8 cells - and now tallying up the total count across all of them.

Since these five shapes sum to exactly 25 cells, I'm testing whether they can tile a 5x5 grid. I'm placing the 8-cell piece in the top rows and working out where the remaining pieces - the V pentomino, the tetromino, and the others - could fit in the leftover cells, particularly checking the rightmost column and lower rows for constraints.

Confirming the count of remaining 12 cells matches the last two pieces (3+4+5=12), then trying to place the row-of-4-with-bump piece along row 4, but the bump keeps landing on already-taken cells, so I try a vertical column-of-4 with bump instead.

That doesn't work either since the resulting shape isn't a valid tetromino match. Let me try the bump at row 2 instead: that leaves an isolated pair at (1,1),(1,2), which also fails to connect properly. I need to try a different piece arrangement entirely.

That row0 setup leaves it isolated with 5 cells, which doesn't match any piece shape, so that fails too. I need to try other rotations of piece 8, like the 180-degree version, and recompute the resulting shape's cells to see if it fits better.

Placing this rotated piece across rows2-4 with the bottom row full, I check the remaining cells: rows0-1 stay full, plus (2,0),(2,3),(2,4),(3,0),(3,2),(3,3),(3,4), totaling 17. The (2,0),(3,0) column connects up to row1 above, so this region stays connected — worth checking against pieces like the L tromino, J tetromino, pentomino, and V piece.

Now testing piece 7 as a J-shape with cells at (1,0),(2,0),(3,0),(1,1) against the reference orientation, comparing the normalized coordinates to see if they match a mirrored version of the target shape.

Rotating the original piece by 180 degrees and normalizing gives me a match with piece 7's shape. But that leaves the remaining five cells in row0 which should belong to piece 2, and that shape doesn't fit the required tiling — so I need to try a different arrangement, perhaps having piece 2 cover part of row0 with its bump placed differently, and restart the placement more systematically.

Trying cols2-4 placement, I calculate the remaining 17 cells left over after placing the rotated 8-piece, then start working out where pieces 5, 7, 2, and 3 could fit into that leftover space.

I place the 3-piece as an L-shape using row0's cells and column3's cells down to row2, leaving 12 cells. Then I try fitting the 2-pentomino along row4 with a bump, checking whether the bump cell lands in an available spot.

With that placed, 7 cells remain for pieces 5 and 7, so I'm testing whether the 7-shape (a column of three plus a foot) fits into the remaining L-shaped region under different rotations.

Trying the r90 orientation placed at rows 0-1 works, covering all four cells there, leaving a tromino remainder that matches an L-tromino shape—checking whether piece 5's rotations can produce that same set, but I need to verify piece 5 is restricted to its original orientation only.

But I realize a bigger issue: the anchor piece must appear in its unrotated orientation in the unique tiling, so I need to check whether a valid tiling exists specifically with piece 8 unrotated, since my current tiling has it rotated 90 degrees.

I'm re-examining the only possible column position for the unrotated shape (starting at column 0), trying row offsets 0 through 2, and checking which of the remaining pieces (5, 7, 2, 3) can fill the leftover cells in each case, starting with row0 and working through the constraints on covering the isolated cells in row1 and row2.

Continuing this branch, the V-tromino works but leaves a plain I-tetromino for piece 7, which needs to be a J instead—so that fails too. Testing the alternative bump position, I try shifting to see if that opens up a valid arrangement for the remaining region.

Since (1,2) can only pair with (1,1), I try piece P={(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)} as the L-shape, which forces (1,0) to connect with (2,0) and the remaining pieces 7,2,3 to cover the rest, testing whether a J-orientation fits at (1,0),(2,0),(3,0),(3,1).

That doesn't work either, so I try piece 3 as a V-shape occupying that column plus a corner bump, leaving nine remaining cells to split between pieces 7 and 2 — but the corner cell (4,0) only has one open neighbor, which keeps blocking every placement I try for the remaining pieces.

Trying the vertical bump variant leaves an I-tetromino for piece 7, which doesn't match, so that fails too. Now I'm checking the subcase where piece 7 occupies cells near (1,1),(1,2), testing which four-cell combinations from the remaining region normalize correctly.

Continuing that path, 12 cells remain for pieces of size 5, 7, and 2. Trying 5 as an L-shape at (2,1),(3,1),(3,2), then 2 covering (1,4),(2,4),(3,4),(4,4) with a bump at (3,3), leaves 7 as a straight I-piece across (4,0)-(4,3) — checking if this tiling works out.

I found a vertical line of 4 plus a bump forming shape 2, leaving an L-tromino for shape 5 — that completes the count. So the full tiling assigns pieces 8, 3, 7, and 2 to their respective cell groups, verifying the whole board is covered correctly.

Now I'm checking each row cell-by-cell to confirm no overlaps between pieces 3, 7, 8, and 2 across rows 1 through 4.

I recall finding an alternate tiling with the 8-piece rotated in columns 2-4, which is fine since uniqueness is defined per anchor orientation — but I need to double-check that this rotated-8 tiling stays consistent with the uniqueness requirement for the other pieces too.

Actually, looking at this more carefully: for anchor 5 in its original orientation, the tiling I found doesn't place 5 that way at all — 5 appears in a different orientation there. So each anchor really does need its own separately-computed tiling, meaning I likely have to work through five distinct constrained tilings rather than reusing one.

I'll try enumerating all tilings of the 5x5 grid with these five pieces under all rotations, tracking piece 8's four rotation options by their coordinate footprints as a starting point for the structural search.

Since piece 8 is 5 units long in one dimension, its placements are limited to three row or column offsets depending on orientation. Now I'm cataloging the input orientations for pieces 5, 7, 2, and 3 to set up anchor cases for each one.

For the anchor 8 case, I'm checking that tiling against each piece's normalized coordinates: 3 forms an L-shape, 7 matches its original input orientation exactly, 2 appears as a vertical line with a bump, and 5 has a simple three-cell shape.

Since 7 already sits in its input orientation within that same tiling, I suspect anchor-7's unique solution might just be identical to anchor-8's. Now I need to check whether anchor 5, anchor 3, and anchor 2 each require different specific orientations of those pieces, which means I need to search for tilings matching each of those constraints separately rather than assuming they all coincide with the same solution.

Checking the 180-rotation confirms this is a valid match, and the remaining pieces confirm this tiling belongs to anchor 3. That leaves me needing tilings for anchor 5 and anchor 2, so I'll start systematically enumerating placements based on where piece 8 goes.

I'm working through the branches where the V-piece covers cells (1,1) and (1,2), checking each possible corner orientation to see if any other configuration besides the one already found actually completes a valid tiling.

Adding (4,0) to {(2,1),(3,1),(4,1)} gives a valid match, but checking the alternative {(2,1),(3,1),(4,2)} normalized shape doesn't match any of the rotation patterns, so I rule that out and continue testing {(2,1),(3,1),(3,2)}.

That other candidate placement also fails since the cell is already taken, confirming rows 0-2 admit exactly one valid tiling for piece 8. But I'm now worried this uniqueness assumption for anchoring piece 7 might not hold across all tilings — I need to double check whether other tilings could also place piece 7 in row 0, which would break the anchor logic.

I'm now checking other placements to see whether they also lead to isolated regions that fail, moving on to try anchor 5 and anchor 2 next.

Trying rows2-4 with cells (2,1),(2,2),(3,1),(4,0..4), leaving 17 cells to fill including rows0-1 fully and a few scattered ones in rows2-3. I'm checking connectivity and isolated corners like (3,2), which only connects through (3,3), to see if a valid pentomino shape can cover that remaining cluster.

Testing a V pentomino for (3,2),(3,3),(3,4),(2,4),(1,4), which fits, then looking at what's left: rows0 fully plus scattered cells in rows1-3 totaling 12 squares, needing pieces 5, 7, and 2. I'm checking (3,0),(2,0),(1,0) as a chain and finding piece 7 rotated 180° fits that column plus one extra cell.

Trying two placements for piece 5 versus 2: one arrangement leaves five cells forming a straight line which fails since I already used the I piece. Switching to placing piece 2 vertically with a single side bump works, leaving seven cells split between rows0 and rows1-2 for pieces 5 and 7 to fill.

Trying {(2,3),(1,3),(0,3),(0,4)} instead: normalized this matches r180, and the leftover cells (0,1),(0,2),(1,2) form an L-tromino matching 5_in. That works, so tiling T2 uses 8_180 across rows 2-4.

Continuing to check the remaining pieces: 2 normalizes to a vertical line with a bump at the third from bottom, which is valid, and 5 matches 5_in again — this seems to correspond to the anchor-5 tiling, assuming it's unique.

Let me also verify piece 3's orientation by normalizing its cells, which gives a corner shape at the bottom-right — different from 3_in, confirming it's a rotation. Now I need to check what orientation 2 requires as an anchor: a horizontal line with a bump below the third cell from the left, and see if this matches any tilings already found.

Checking the anchor-3 and anchor-5 tilings, their 2 pieces don't match this required orientation (one gives a bump above column 1, the other is vertical), so I need to search further placements — specifically the 8_90 and 8_270 orientations across different column offsets, working through where a full column plus adjacent bump cells could land.

For c0=0, splitting the board into a 7-cell left region and 10-cell right region, I check that (4,0),(4,1) end up isolated with only 2 connected cells, so this placement fails. Moving to c0=1, I'm now tracing which cells remain free after placing the full column and bump cells there.

Trying a horizontal 4-piece across row0 with a bump into (1,3), which fits. That leaves 12 cells for the 5,7,3 pieces, and I find a valid V-shaped placement for the 3-piece using (1,4),(2,4),(3,4),(3,3),(3,2), narrowing remaining cells further.

Checking that arrangement, (2,3) ends up isolated with no open neighbors, so it fails. I try alternate V orientations for the 3-piece anchored near (2,3)/(2,4)/(1,4), but corner arm placements keep hitting taken cells, so I'm testing another configuration where the 7-piece covers (1,4),(2,4),(2,3) plus extensions.

Trying {(1,4),(2,4),(2,3)} as a valid L-tromino works, leaving nine cells for the remaining pieces. I place the V-piece at (2,1),(3,1),(4,1),(4,2),(4,3), which fits, and the leftover cells (3,2),(3,3),(3,4),(4,4) normalize into a valid r270 shape matching piece 7 — success.

Now I'm checking a complete solution: piece 8 covers a large L-shape along the left column, piece 2 covers the top row plus one cell, piece 5 covers three cells, piece 3 covers the V-shape, and piece 7 covers the remaining four. I'm going cell by cell to verify no overlaps or gaps across the full grid.

Building the grid...

I finish assembling the anchor-5 tiling grid and verify the 8-cell count matches, then start laying out the anchor-2 tiling variant.

Next I map each square from the tiling back onto the actual output grid by computing offsets so each anchor piece keeps its original position, working through square 5's coordinate translation as an example calculation.

Now I'm placing the 7-anchor square using the same offset method: matching input cells (3,19),(4,19),(5,18),(5,19) against tiling A's shape to compute rows 1-5, cols 18-22 for that square.

Then I move to anchor 2: matching input cells (10,3)-(10,6),(11,5) against tiling D's shape, computing dr=10, dc=2 to place square D starting at row 10.

I confirm the mapping at (11,5), then fill in rows 10-14 with the corresponding D-square values.

Next I tackle anchor 3, matching input cells (12,15)-(14,17) to tiling B's shape, finding dr=12, dc=14, and start filling rows 12-16 with B's values.

Then for anchor 8, I match the input cells around row19-21 to tiling A, computing dr=19, dc=5, and fill rows 19-23 with A's values, verifying the mapping checks out.

Now I need to recount the input grid carefully since it has 26 rows of 25 columns, not the count I assumed, so I'm re-verifying row indices against the original listing to make sure my shape positions align correctly.

Filling in the output grid row by row, placing the small 8-pattern block near columns 18-22 in the top rows, then the 2/5/7 block and 7/5/2 mirrored block spanning columns 7-11 and 18-22 in the middle rows.

Continuing down, I'm mapping out rows 15-23 with another pair of shifting colored blocks (5,2,8 and 2,2,2 patterns, then 8,3,7,5,2 sequences), with rows 17-18 and 24-25 empty, then compiling the full 25-row grid.

I'm checking the areas of these shapes and finding that shape 3, 7, and 2 together sum to 25, forming a 5x5 square. Now I'm mapping out how shape 3 fills its portion of that grid row by row.

Working through the remaining 7 cells, I test rotations to fit the T-tetromino and L-tromino pieces together: placing the T at four cells and confirming the L fills the leftover three cells cleanly, then translating both into actual grid coordinates.

But then I catch a problem: the T-tetromino's orientation in this placement is a rotated version of its original shape, and if the anchor requires the piece to stay in its fixed original orientation, this arrangement doesn't actually satisfy the constraint. That means this whole candidate grouping might be invalid, forcing me to reconsider whether any valid tiling exists at all for this anchor.

I'm checking whether the T-shape can fit inside this 7-cell region shape under any of its four rotations, since the region itself has an asymmetric notch cut from a 3x3 square. Testing the region in its base orientation, the T's nub doesn't align with the available cells, so I need to rotate the region and re-check each case systematically.

Rotating 180° gives a set forming T with nub at (1,1), and the remainder forms an L tromino — that works! Now checking the 270° rotation's cell mapping.

I'm working out the T and L piece placements and orientations, checking whether the anchor-3 tiling is also unique, then mapping out the grid rows 2-6 across columns 7-11 to fill in where each piece (3, 7, 2) lands cell by cell.

Now I'm constructing the second placement by rotating the 3-shape 180 degrees within a 5x5 grid, translating each occupied cell coordinate to figure out the new row/column layout for the rotated configuration.

Mapping this back into the actual grid, I position the square starting at (14,8) and work out which cells get labeled 7, 3, or 2 across rows 14-15, verifying the T and L sub-shapes land correctly.

For placement 3, the L piece needs to sit in a fixed orientation at (16,16),(16,17),(17,16), so I'm checking each rotation of the R region to find which one contains an L matching that exact cell pattern, then seeing what's left over for the T piece.

Checking R180 next: trying different splits into L-tetromino plus T-tetromino, but each split leaves disconnected cells or an L shape instead of a T, so R180 fails too. Moving on to check R270 the same way.

I need to figure out the position of the 3x3 region within the 5x5 grid and apply the rotation transformation directly to the full grid coordinates instead of the local 3x3 ones, then take the complement to get the R270 configuration.

That gives 7 cells in rows2-4, cols0-2, confirming it matches the cw-rotated shape. Now I need the complement to equal the ccw rotation instead, so I'm applying (r,c)→(4-c,r) to the original 3-shape to check that mapping.

Now I'm mapping anchor 2 at (16,16) into the offset region, translating the L, T, and 3-shapes into their new grid coordinates and confirming each matches its expected color, continuing the col0-4 translation into cols14-18 rows16-20.

Then I'm building the 24x24 output grid, filling in the first placement at rows2-6, cols7-11 with the 3, 2, and 7 colors according to the mapped shapes, and starting the second placement at rows14-18, cols8-12 with the same pattern shifted.

Finishing rows17-18 of placement2 with all 3s across cols8-12, then mapping placement3 at rows16-20, cols14-18, verifying each row's mix of 3s, 2s, and 7s matches the pattern, confirming row18's values line up correctly.

I'm trying to design simple shape pairs to test the partition rule—since a valid partition needs either one group of 3+ shapes or two groups of 2, I'm working out an example using two groups of two shapes each that combine into 2x2 squares, like an L-tromino paired with a single cell.

But identical shapes across groups (like two dominoes) share the same signature and get rejected, so I need distinct shapes per group. I'm settling on a 3x3 grid split into a square tetromino, an L-tetromino, and a single cell, verifying that a corner 2x2 block plus the remaining L-shaped region tiles correctly with those pieces.

For a second grouping I try a 3x3 with an I-tromino, a domino, and a tetromino, checking that placing the I-tromino as a column leaves a clean 3x2 region for the other two pieces.

I sketch out grid coordinates for each color region across two 14x14 test grids, placing squares, L-shapes, and singles at spaced-out positions to verify tiling correctness.
